questions.question: What is a dataclass in Python, and how do type hints make it better?
questions.title: Typed Dataclasses in Python
questions.direct_answer: @dataclass auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for a class that mainly holds data, removing boilerplate. With type hints, the fields are annotated (name: str, age: int), which makes the dataclass self-documenting, gives IDE autocomplete, and lets mypy check that you pass the right types. A dataclass is the idiomatic way to model a typed record (a User, a Config) in modern Python — far less boilerplate than a manual __init__, and safer than a dict because the type checker validates it.

sections.title: Auto-Generated Methods for a Data Class
sections.content: @dataclass (from the dataclasses module) auto-generates the boilerplate methods — __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ — for a class that mainly holds data, so you write just the fields. With type hints, each field is annotated (name: str, age: int), which makes the dataclass self-documenting, gives IDE autocomplete, and lets mypy check that you pass the right types when constructing or mutating. A dataclass is the idiomatic way to model a typed record (a User, a Config) in modern Python — far less boilerplate than a manual __init__, and safer than a dict because the type checker validates the fields. You can add methods and defaults, and use frozen=True for immutability.

sections.title: A Dataclass vs a Manual Class
sections.content:
@dataclass writes __init__/__repr__/__eq__ for you; type-annotated fields enable mypy checks.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F[name: str, age: int] -->|@dataclass| A[auto __init__/__repr__/__eq__]
  F -->|annotated| M[mypy checks construction]
  A --> U[User = User\('Ada', 36\)]
```

sections.title: A typed dataclass vs a manual class
sections.content:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

# (1) TYPED DATACLASS: fields annotated; methods auto-generated.
@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    age: int
    active: bool = True          # a default

u = User("Ada", 36)              # __init__ auto-generated
print(u)                         # User(name='Ada', age=36, active=True)  (__repr__)
u2 = User("Ada", 36)
print(u == u2)                   # True  (__eq__ auto-generated by field values)

# (2) FROZEN dataclass = immutable (hashable, can be a dict key).
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: float
    y: float
#   Point(1,2).x = 9  -> raises FrozenInstanceError
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Writing a manual __init__ and __repr__ for a data class — the exact boilerplate @dataclass removes.
A mutable default (field: list = []) shared across instances — use field(default_factory=list).
Forgetting frozen=True when you need immutability/hashing (e.g., a dict key or set member).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: @dataclass auto-generates __init__, __repr__, and __eq__ for a class that mainly holds data.
Type-annotated fields (name: str) make the dataclass self-documenting and mypy-checkable.
It's the idiomatic typed record in modern Python — far less boilerplate than a manual __init__.
Use frozen=True for immutability (and hashing — frozen dataclasses can be dict keys).
For mutable defaults use field(default_factory=list), not a shared list literal.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: dataclass, from the dataclasses module, auto-generates the boilerplate methods — init, repr, and eq — for a class that mainly holds data, so you write just the fields. With type hints, each field is annotated, like name colon str and age colon int, which makes the dataclass self-documenting, gives IDE autocomplete, and lets mypy check that you pass the right types when constructing or mutating. A dataclass is the idiomatic way to model a typed record, like a User or a Config, in modern Python — far less boilerplate than a manual init, and safer than a dict because the type checker validates the fields. You can add methods and defaults, and use frozen equals True for immutability, which also makes the dataclass hashable so it can be a dict key or set member. The common mistakes are writing a manual init and repr for a data class, which is the exact boilerplate dataclass removes, using a mutable default like field colon list equals empty-list which is shared across instances — you should use field of default_factory equals list instead — and forgetting frozen equals True when you need immutability or hashing.
